name: Birthday-number effect
statement: People rate the numbers in their own birth date, the day and the month, as more likeable than other numbers.
meaning: The claim is about liking, not about use. Shown a run of numbers and asked how much each appeals to them, people put the day and the month of their own birth above the rest. Three separate claims travel together. The first is that preference, measured on a rating scale. The second is that the preference indexes self-esteem a respondent cannot manage, which turns the rating task into an instrument called the birthday number task. The third is that the preference steers decisions in the world, over where people live, what they pay and whom they marry. Each stands or falls on its own evidence. The letter version of the same argument is covered under the name-letter effect, and the career and marriage disputes it feeds are covered under nominative determinism.

origin.note: The paper is "Implicit self-esteem in Japan: Name letters and birthday numbers", pages 736 to 742 of volume 23. It paired a letter-rating study with a number-rating study, and its question was why Japanese samples show no explicit self-enhancement. It sits behind a paywall these checks did not pass, so what it did is described here from two papers that were read. Simonsohn reports that its number effect was much smaller, and not reliable, for numbers below 12. Nutt, DiMassimo and Hale report that it covered month, day and year, and that it found higher numbers rated above lower ones.

evidence: Bosson, Swann and Pennebaker ran the task on 84 University of Texas undergraduates, 40 men and 44 women, with one excluded. Participants rated every letter of the alphabet and the numbers 0 through 35 on a seven-point liking scale. A birthday-preference score subtracts the number's average popularity across all raters from the owner's own rating of it, so a person born on 19 November is scored on 19. The mean came to 0.73 scale points, SD 1.54, t(80) = 4.28. The initials version of the same task on the same people came to 0.93, t(80) = 6.13. Nickell, Pederson and Rossow put 83 participants through a broader set of dates and objects and report a more positive evaluation of the birth month and birth year than of other months and years, which they read as an extension of the mere ownership effect. Stieger and Krizan rated numbers in six countries, N = 657, and found the preference bending to local custom: whether Christmas falls on 24 or 25 December moved the liking of those two numbers, and numerals used for good school grades were liked above numerals used for bad ones. The field claim starts elsewhere. Pelham, Mirenberg and Jones asked in their Study 6 whether people live in towns whose names carry their birthday number, and of 485 people in their sample 94 died in a matching town against 70 expected, a ratio of actual to expected frequency of 1.33, p < .001. Those figures are Simonsohn's account of that study.

replication.headline: The rating-task preference repeats in fresh samples; the archival claims built on it do not.
replication.detail: Nutt, DiMassimo and Hale ran the closest thing to a direct repeat of the original design, on 101 students at the University of North Georgia rating the numbers 1 to 50 among distractor items. Birthday numbers were rated above other numbers, F(1, 97) = 17.85, p < .001, partial eta squared .16. Month and day did not differ, F(1, 97) = 0.23, p = .64, and the split between numbers 1 to 12 and 13 to 31 fell short at F(1, 97) = 3.68, p = .06, against the original report that the effect belongs to the larger numbers. Their self-esteem test came out flat, r(99) = -.02, p = .88. The archival side goes the other way. Simonsohn took the whole Social Security Death Index, N = 80.4 million, and asked whether the day of a person's birthday predicts living in a town named for that number. He found 967 matches against 954.5 expected, a ratio of 1.01, p = .46. He then used a New York voter registration file of 12.8 million people to test birthday numbers against street name, address number and apartment number. Not one of the 21 chi-square tests reached the 5% level, and the pooled ratios were .98, 1.01 and 1.01, with p values of .74, .73 and .50. He notes that his matching counts run 8 to 20 times larger than the originals and his samples 10,000 to 30,000 times larger. His reading is that the laboratory effect is real and too small to move a decision about where to live.

study.cite: Nutt, C. G., DiMassimo, A. N., & Hale, R. G. (2024). Revisiting the birthday number effect, subjective preferences, and self-esteem in college students. Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research, 29(2), 120-128.

limits: The measure is weak where it is used as a measure. In Bosson's sample the birthday task correlated -.10, .17, .00 and .00 with four explicit self-esteem scales, none of them reliable, and .23 with the initials task run on the same people. Its retest correlation over a mean of 31.23 days was .53, against .80 for the Rosenberg scale. Falk, Heine, Takemura, Zhang and Hsu gave the birthday number task with the numbers 1 to 40 to Euro-Canadians, Asian-Canadians and Japanese, 107, 187 and 112 people, and again to 582 Americans. Among Asian-Canadians the task correlated with explicit self-esteem at a mean of -.15, and the authors conclude that implicit self-esteem measures are not valid for individual or cross-cultural comparison. Blanton and Jaccard's argument about arbitrary metrics is relevant to what such a score could mean, though their worked case is the Implicit Association Test rather than number preference. No preregistered or large-sample test of the basic preference was located. The nearest large test is behavioural: D'Hondt, Roger, Hoffmann and Plotkina report a stronger birthday-number effect in women than men among Belgian lotto players, and its disappearance on a second ticket filled in straight after the first, which they read as a matter of response speed rather than automaticity. That paper was read at its abstract. Four items could not be obtained. Kitayama and Karasawa's own numbers are paywalled, as are Jones, Pelham, Mirenberg and Hetts, whose 2002 paper extended the letter finding to birthday numbers, Pelham and Carvallo's 2015 marriage analyses, and Keller and Gierl's 2017 attempt on the advertising claim.
misreadings: Simonsohn is read as having overturned the effect. He did not test it. He calls the laboratory evidence for own-name and own-number preference abundant and convincing, and says the effect may act where a chooser is close to indifferent, which is not how a town or a spouse is chosen. The instrument and the phenomenon are also collapsed. Failures of the birthday number task as a self-esteem measure say nothing about whether people like their own numbers, and the liking says nothing about what the task measures. The scoring rule is narrower than the name suggests: Bosson's version scores the day alone, Kitayama and Karasawa's covered month and day, and Nickell's covered month and year, so three studies under one heading count three different things. The commercial extension is a claim of its own. Coulter and Grewal report that prices whose cents digits match a buyer's birth date raise liking and purchase intention, to the point of a higher-priced product beating a cheaper one, and their paper is the source for that claim rather than any of the rating studies.
